title: As ... As: Describing People
why: Native speakers use as ... as similes every day to sum up a person in a few vivid words. Knowing the exact animal or object in each one, and where it is used, stops you sounding either textbook or foreign.
know: the frame as + adjective + as + noun and the fixed noun in each simile
eight common similes for character, health and mood
understand: why the comparison noun can't be swapped freely, even when another animal seems logical
which similes are North American, which are British, and which sound old-fashioned or cliched
able: describe people's personality, health and mood vividly but naturally
drop the first as in casual speech and recognise playful variations
avoid stacking cliches and choose one simile that really fits
mistakes: She stayed as cool like a cucumber during the inspection.
She stayed as cool as a cucumber. The frame is always as ... as, never as ... like.
My grandfather is as fit as a violin at ninety.
As fit as a fiddle. The noun is fixed, even though a fiddle and a violin are the same instrument.
My boss is as stubborn as a donkey.
As stubborn as a mule. A literal translation (e.g. from German) is understood, but English uses mule.
The new intern is as quiet as a mice.
As quiet as a mouse. The noun is singular with a.
Our CEO is as sharp as a tack, as busy as a bee and as cool as a cucumber.
Choose one simile. Stacking cliches sounds like a parody or a weak reference letter.
bigidea: A simile compares two things openly with as or like; a metaphor simply says one thing is another. He's as stubborn as a mule is a simile; he's a mule is a metaphor, and it sounds much ruder.

The as + adjective + as + noun frame works as an intensifier: as proud as a peacock just means extremely proud, with a picture attached. Because the picture does the work, the noun is usually fixed by tradition, and changing it sounds odd.
Many of these similes are old and slightly folksy, so they're best in conversation, stories and light writing. In casual speech the first as often disappears: cool as a cucumber, fit as a fiddle.
hidden: My aunt has a memory like an elephant; she never forgets a birthday.
He hardly touched his dinner. He eats like a bird.
When they called his name he went as red as a beetroot.
She was shaking like a leaf before her driving test.
You look like a million bucks in that suit.
Our coach has eyes like a hawk; nothing gets past her.
Grandpa was like a kid in a candy store at the hardware show.

expressions.meaning: extremely unwilling to change your mind or behaviour
expressions.example: Dad is as stubborn as a mule; he still won't use a GPS.
expressions.bend: Often shortened: stubborn as a mule. Also mule-headed. Usually critical, but can be affectionate in families.
expressions.note: Trap: not as stubborn as a donkey or as a goat. Near-synonym pig-headed is ruder.

expressions.meaning: very quiet, shy or making almost no noise
expressions.example: The new analyst was as quiet as a mouse for her first month.
expressions.bend: Describes people or how they move: she crept up the stairs as quiet as a mouse. Also mousy (shy and dull, unkind).
expressions.note: Neutral or kind, unlike mousy. Don't confuse with as poor as a church mouse, which is about money and old-fashioned.

expressions.example: He walked around the wedding as proud as a peacock after his speech.
expressions.bend: Fixed noun. Also the verb to peacock (show off) and preen. Often lightly mocking.
expressions.note: Can be warm (a proud parent) or critical (vanity). Context and tone of voice decide.

expressions.meaning: very calm and relaxed, especially under pressure
expressions.example: The pilot stayed as cool as a cucumber during the emergency landing.
expressions.bend: Very often without the first as: cool as a cucumber. Always a cucumber.
expressions.note: Admiring. About calm, not about being fashionable. Near-synonym: calm, cool and collected.

expressions.meaning: in very good health, often said of older people
expressions.example: After the hip replacement, Mum is as fit as a fiddle again.
expressions.bend: Fit as a fiddle in casual speech. Usually after be, feel or look.
expressions.note: A slightly old-fashioned, cheerful phrase. Fit once meant suitable or in good condition, like a well-tuned fiddle.

expressions.meaning: very busy, working actively and cheerfully
expressions.example: With three grandchildren visiting, I've been as busy as a bee all week.
expressions.bend: Related noun: a busy bee (she's a real busy bee). Not as busy like a bee.
expressions.note: Positive: productive and energetic. If you mean stressed and overloaded, swamped or snowed under is better.

expressions.example: Our MP is as sharp as a tack; she remembers every figure.
expressions.bend: Mainly North American. British speakers say as sharp as a knife or as sharp as a razor; razor-sharp works everywhere.
expressions.note: Often used for older people who are still mentally quick: at 95 he's still sharp as a tack. A tack is a small pin.

expressions.example: Give him a lawn chair and a fishing rod and he's as happy as a clam.
expressions.bend: North American. The British and Australian version is as happy as Larry. Also happy as a pig in mud (very informal).
expressions.note: Originally longer: happy as a clam at high tide, when it's safe from diggers. The short form is what people say now.

culture.how: Burns opens with two famous like similes: his love is compared to a rose newly opened in early summer and to a sweetly played tune. He then promises to love her until the seas dry up. It's the classic example of a simile used for a person.
culture.ask: If you had to compare someone you love to a flower or a piece of music, which would you choose and why?
culture.find: Robert Burns A Red Red Rose

culture.how: Chaucer introduces each pilgrim with quick comparisons. The young Squire is said to be as fresh as the month of May, while the brawny Miller has a beard as red as a sow or a fox. Six hundred years ago, English already described people this way.
culture.ask: Describe someone you know in one simile, the way Chaucer does. Is it kind or mocking?

culture.how: The Hatter and the March Hare host the famous mad tea party. Carroll didn't invent as mad as a hatter or as mad as a March hare: the hare simile goes back to the early 1500s, and the Nova Scotian writer Thomas Chandler Haliburton used the hatter one in The Clockmaker in the 1830s. Carroll turned both similes into characters.
culture.ask: The hatter link to mercury poisoning is only a theory. Why do you think such origin stories are so popular?
culture.find: mad as a hatter origin Haliburton Clockmaker

culture.how: The title simile drives the song. Dylan addresses a woman who grew up privileged and looked down on others, and who now has no home and no direction. A rolling stone, from the old proverb about gathering no moss, stands for someone with nothing to hold on to.
culture.ask: Is Dylan's simile sympathetic, cruel or both? What makes you think so?

pick.why: Showing obvious pride = as proud as a peacock.

spot.q: The surgeon stayed as cool as an ice cube when the power failed.
spot.bad: as cool as an ice cube
spot.why: The fixed simile is cool as a cucumber: calm under pressure.

spot.q: After six weeks of physiotherapy, my brother is as fit as a violin.
spot.why: Same instrument, but only fiddle works in the simile.

spot.q: The old professor is still as sharp as a nail at eighty-eight.
spot.why: Sharp as a tack (North American) or as sharp as a knife (British). Not a nail.

spot.q: During tax season my accountant is as busy like a bee.
spot.why: The frame is as ... as. Never mix as with like.

spot.q: He's as happy as a fish now that he works from home.

type.q: I asked her three times to see a doctor, but she's as stubborn as a ___.
type.why: As stubborn as a mule: refusing to change.

type.q: The new tenant upstairs is as quiet as a ___; we barely know he's there.
type.why: As quiet as a mouse: making almost no noise.

type.q: Look at him in his new uniform, as proud as a ___.
type.why: As proud as a peacock: showing obvious pride.

type.q: The goalie was cool as a ___ in the shootout.
type.why: Cool as a cucumber: calm under pressure. The first as is often dropped.

type.q: I had the flu last week, but now I'm as fit as a ___.
type.why: As fit as a fiddle: in excellent health.

type.q: At 97 my grandmother is still sharp as a ___ and beats us all at cribbage.
type.why: Sharp as a tack: mentally quick. North American.

bend.q: A friend is describing a calm pilot in casual speech. Which version sounds natural? ___
opts: She was cool as a cucumber the whole time.
She was cool like as a cucumber the whole time.
She was as cool than a cucumber the whole time.
bend.why: Dropping the first as is very natural in casual speech. Like as and than are wrong.

bend.q: A British colleague is describing a retired friend. Which version would she most likely use? ___
opts: He's as happy as a Larry in his garden.
He's as happy as Larry in his garden.
He's as happy like Larry in his garden.
bend.why: British English: as happy as Larry, with no article.

bend.q: Which version uses the related noun naturally to praise a volunteer? ___
opts: My aunt is a real busy bee.
My aunt is a real busy as a bee.
My aunt is a real bee of busy.
bend.why: A busy bee is the noun form. A real adds friendly emphasis.

bend.q: Which version sounds natural about a whole team that refuses a new rule? ___
opts: They're as stubborn as mules about it.
They're as stubborn as a mules about it.
They're stubborn as mule about it.
bend.why: With a plural subject you can say as mules. No a with a plural, and don't drop the article with the singular.

talk: Chaucer describes his pilgrims in a word or two. Describe three people in your family with one simile each. Are your similes kind, teasing or critical?
Burns compares his love to a rose and a melody. Do similes like these sound romantic or cliched to you today? What would a modern love simile be?
Role-play: you're writing a reference for a former employee. Your tutor says you overused cliches. Rewrite it out loud using at most one simile.
Which of today's similes exist in your language with a different animal or object? Explain the differences to your tutor.
Dylan's title compares a person to a rolling stone. Is it better to be a rolling stone or to gather moss? Use at least two similes from this lesson.
